fix.note: Published 29 October 2026 at 12:47 am IST, updated 7:09 am, by Himanshi Dahiya, with the full text served on the page. This is the report The Wire's piece of 29 October 2026, 'BJP and EC Said SIR Was to Remove ‘Infiltrators’. A Report Shows it Recorded Just 1,600 Foreigners' (The Wire Staff, 11:32 am), relies on, and The Wire adds to it only Amit Shah's remark of 2025, a line on the protests and its own words that the SIR 'has now deleted 13 crore names', so the original is listed in its place. The 1,600 is not an official figure and no official document gives it. It is the paper's own sum of counts given to it by officials of six Chief Electoral Officers' offices (716 + about 500 + 419 + 3 + 2 + 0 = about 1,640), and the senior Commission official it quotes says the Commission holds no combined or state-wise figure. The Karnataka 716 is attributed to an official of the state Chief Electoral Officer's office, and the Chief Electoral Officer himself said only that the number was less than 1,000. The News Minute of 29 October credits the 716 to the Times of India. The roll figures the paper gives agree with data/india/states.json: Karnataka 99.7 lakh fewer on the final roll (99,76,625 general electors), Kerala 8,97,211 and Goa 1,27,468 fewer, Meghalaya 1,65,682 fewer and a final roll of 21.8 lakh, Mizoram about 39,000 fewer (39,199), Jharkhand 2.646 crore before and 43.6 lakh left off the draft. The 9.86 crore is the sum of the six states' latest rolls (Karnataka final, Jharkhand draft, the other four final). The Reporters' Collective's piece of 16 October 2026 on the absence of any foreigner category is already on the reading list.

fix.shows: Sravasti Dasgupta reads the Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 against The Indian Express's reports that Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu objected 14 times in ten months, and finds that it denies none of those findings. By her account the affidavit says the Commission neither released nor authorised the release of any internal note, and that all three orders for the SIR were reached unanimously. It denies that Form 6 was amended while accepting that the declaration was entered into the online page of the form, and it now calls the declaration a separate and independent document, where a press note of the month before had said the declaration attached to Form 6 was upheld by the Supreme Court. She writes that on Goa it says 88 of the 97 voters have applied again through Form 6 and does not explain why registration officers could not restore them, and that on West Bengal it says the appeals were not brought to the Commission. It announces a committee with experts from IIT Mumbai and IISc Bengaluru to review new ECINet modules without mentioning that Joshi had proposed one, and it calls the allegations drawn from the two Commissioners' letters to the Cabinet Secretary about a work allocation order misconceived, saying the order was never implemented.

note: Second reading, 29 October 2026: read afresh in full from The Wire's post data (post_date 28 October 2026 00:56:30, author Sravasti Dasgupta, title as given). The summary holds, with one change. The piece says the affidavit calls 'the allegations based on these communications' misconceived, meaning the two Commissioners' letters to the Cabinet Secretary, so the summary now says that. fix.shows: Human Rights Watch says it has interviewed 70 people in Delhi, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Karnataka since August, among them 40 whose families were affected by the revision, former election commissioners, lawyers, activists and a serving electoral official. It finds that people were excluded for mismatched names, spelling errors, having six or more siblings or siblings born less than nine months apart, and that the software flagged Adivasi and Muslim names disproportionately, in part because their spellings vary. It finds that the authorities used data from the revision to deny passport renewals, food rations, a West Bengal cash transfer for women, scholarships and residence certificates, including to people whose appeals were still pending. It describes the bulk use of Form 7 against Muslim voters as the media reported it, transgender people excluded because their documents carry different names, and security forces beating and arresting protesters in October 2026. Its Asia director, Elaine Pearson, calls for the revision to be scrapped and for everyone wrongly excluded to regain the vote promptly.
fix.note: Published 28 October 2026 at 11:30 pm EDT (29 October in India), datelined London, and labelled Report on the page. Its Patharpratima figure of over 92% Muslim among those deleted, against 9% of the population, links to a Scroll report on Nandigram, which gives 95.5% of the deletions in seven supplementary lists against a population 25% Muslim and does not mention Patharpratima.

fix.shows: Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav put Uttar Pradesh's adult population at an estimated 16.2 crore on 1 March 2026 against 13.4 crore names on the final roll of April 2026, down from 15.4 crore before the revision, and conclude that about 2.8 crore voters, or 17.3% of adults, appear to be missing. They reply to Surjit Bhalla's estimate of a shortfall of 20 lakh, which treats all non-enrolment as voluntary and builds on the nearly 40% of the state's adults aged 18 to 29 who were not enrolled in 2024, and say that with the figure for 2019 his shortfall would be 93 lakh. As further evidence they cite the State Election Commission's parallel revision of the rural roll, which ended at 12.6 crore and, with the unrevised urban list of 2023, gives 16.9 crore voters in the state. They hold that the final roll seems to fail on completeness, equity and accuracy, and that the shortfall works against women and young voters.

The states.json comparisons in the note are right: 15,44,30,092 before, 13,39,84,792 final on 10 April 2026, 16,16,85,000 adults, a gap of 2,77,00,208 or 17.1%, 2,88,74,067 left off the draft and a net fall of 2,04,45,300. fix.shows: Bishwajit Bhattacharyya, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court and a former Additional Solicitor General of India, argues that the Court erred in its verdict of 27 May 2026 by allowing the Commission a limited inquiry into citizenship when it includes or deletes names. In his reading the words limited and strict sense carry no legal significance, and the holding that the Commission's power affects an individual's entitlement to be on the roll can only mean that it may disenfranchise an existing voter. He says the Commission's role in preparing the roll is ministerial, that the verdict named no document as proof of citizenship, and that a qualified voter can be disqualified only on the grounds in Article 326 and only after a hearing. He asks how a roll used in a concluded election can be altered on suspicion, urges the Court to lay down a yardstick for establishing citizenship, and reads three earlier judgments as making the right to vote a basic feature of the Constitution.

note: Second reading, 29 October 2026: read afresh in full from the article body in the page's structured data (headline as given, author Bishwajit Bhattacharyya, published 12:16 am IST, modified 12:38 pm, isAccessibleForFree false, so the subscription flag is right). fix.shows: The News Minute sets the final roll of 4,54,55,689 general electors against about 5.19 crore people old enough to vote in a projected Karnataka population of about 6.89 crore on 1 March 2026, and finds the roll about 64.5 lakh short. It cites the Chief Electoral Officer's elector to population ratio of 66.11. By its calculation 38.41 lakh of the shortfall, or 59.5%, are aged 18 to 29. It reports the Chief Electoral Officer, V. Anbu Kumar, saying that out of more than 43.82 lakh notices for logical discrepancies and unmapped entries at least 1,88,324 names were deleted from the final roll, with 61,867 marked ineligible, and that the foreign nationals found number less than a thousand and are still being identified. It cites the Times of India for a figure of 716 foreign nationals, and reports that the Commission has ordered special drives and a fresh look at constituencies, wards and booths where deletions were high.
